clue.text: Whips that go with forage caps ?

definitions.text: Whips that go with forage caps ?

parts.words: Whips that go with forage caps ?
parts.note: a forage cap is a soldier's cap, but read 'forage' as hunting for harvest produce and these riding whips belong with it

explanation.surface: A quartermaster asks which whips are issued alongside the soldiers' forage caps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forage caps' looks like military kit; the pun splits it as foraging, i.e. hunting, for crops, which is exactly what the whips' name says.
explanation.definitionFit: Short riding whips with a loop, carried in the field by riders following hounds.

clue.text: Harry Percy comes up short for a change

indicators.note: a change of order means the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Harry Percy rises with a short-changed purse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a change' rearranges UPSHORT. Sir Henry Percy, Shakespeare's rash rebel in Henry IV Part 1, was nicknamed for his hot temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Percy, the fiery rebel of Henry IV Part 1, bore this nickname.

clue.text: Charles's bird

parts.note: bird is slang for girlfriend, and King Charles II's mistress was the actress Gwyn, known by this pet name

explanation.surface: We are told about a man's pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' suggests a feathered pet; in British slang it means a girlfriend, and Charles II's famous mistress was Nell Gwyn. The word is also a name for the giant petrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Pet name of Nell Gwyn, mistress of King Charles II, and also a seabird, the giant petrel.

clue.text: Perform with a tool

definitions.meaning: carry out, as in putting a plan into effect
an instrument or utensil used for work

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to carry out a plan; as a noun, a utensil or instrument for a job.

clue.text: Get along, funny man

definitions.meaning: an exhortation to carry on or proceed, or to fare
a member of the 1950s radio comedy team of Milligan, Sellers and Secombe

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it means proceed; as one, a comic of The Goon Show, the famous BBC radio comedy, or a clown.

clue.text: Fodder sources of bread and milk

parts.note: rye is a grain that is ground for bread, so it is a source of it
cows turn grazed pasture into milk, so pasture is milk's source

explanation.surface: A farmer lists where bread and milk ultimately come from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' joins the two sources: one cereal for loaves, one pasture plant that cows turn into milk.
explanation.definitionFit: A grass grown for hay and pasture to feed livestock.

clue.text: Dad on rearing mount lacks our faith

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase for a heathen, a person outside the faith

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: in a down clue a horse rearing up reads from the bottom upward, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a nag is a horse, something one mounts to ride

explanation.surface: A father on a horse that rears up turns out to be an unbeliever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rearing' turns NAG upward into GAN; the definition is a description of someone outside Christianity.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone who does not hold the Christian religion.

clue.text: Share swimming-pool with Aguecheek? Such a comedown!

definitions.note: the definition is an exclamation describing something marked by an anticlimax

parts.note: to use a swimming pool is to swim or bathe in it
ague is a fit of shivering, and a twitch of the cheek is a facial spasm, so the name suggests a facial twitch

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified at having to share a swimming pool with Shakespeare's foolish knight.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Andrew Aguecheek is the foolish knight in Twelfth Night; here the name is broken into ague (shaking) and cheek, i.e. a facial twitch. Bathos is a ludicrous descent from the sublime.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathos is a sudden anticlimactic drop from the lofty to the trivial, an absurd letdown.

clue.text: This sort of figure for a wicket-keeper?

definitions.text: This sort of figure for a wicket-keeper

parts.words: This sort of figure for a wicket-keeper
parts.note: a wicket-keeper in cricket stands behind the stumps, so a short thickset build suits him

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what body shape suits a cricket wicket-keeper.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the wicket-keeper crouches behind the three stumps, the wooden posts of the wicket, hence the pun on a short, stocky figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Short and thick in build, punning on the stumps a wicket-keeper guards.

clue.text: On which one gets strung up — no way!

definitions.text: On which one gets strung up — no way

parts.words: On which one gets strung up — no way
parts.note: take 'strung up' with no way (ST, street) and you are left with 'rung up', which is what happens to a caller on this device

explanation.surface: Someone protests in horror at the idea of being hanged on a gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strung up' suggests a hanging; removing ST (an abbreviation for street, so 'way') leaves 'rung up'. The wires carrying the line are also strung up on poles.
explanation.definitionFit: A device for calling people over a line, so someone is rung up on it.

clue.text: Bribery in the nursery ?

definitions.meaning: corrupt payments, in a sense common in American political slang
a plant nursery, where gardeners join a shoot onto rootstock

explanation.definitionFit: Graft is both corrupt dealing for gain and the gardener's technique of splicing a scion onto a stock, practised in plant nurseries.

clue.text: There is still one for Bill in hospital

definitions.text: There is still one for Bill in hospital

parts.words: There is still one for Bill in hospital
parts.note: Bill reads as a man's name, but it is the invoice: a private patient's place in an NHS hospital still comes with a bill

explanation.surface: A friend reassures us that a hospital still has room for a patient called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man; it is the charge. After the NHS was founded, some hospital places remained available to private, fee-paying patients.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed in a state hospital reserved for a private patient who is charged for treatment.

clue.text: Hand out sandwich-filling in Lincs

definitions.note: the definition is a place in Lincolnshire, so a noun for a town there

parts.note: to grant is to give or hand out
ham is a classic thing to put in a sandwich

explanation.surface: Someone is distributing sandwiches in Lincolnshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincs is the abbreviation for Lincolnshire, an English county; the definition is just 'in Lincs', i.e. somewhere located there.
explanation.definitionFit: Grantham is a market town in Lincolnshire, birthplace of Margaret Thatcher.

clue.text: One galosh that's the best of three?

definitions.meaning: a single waterproof overshoe, which Americans call by this name
a series of three games in bridge or whist, won by taking two

explanation.definitionFit: A rubber is an overshoe (US) and also a set of games in bridge or cricket decided by the majority.

clue.text: Robert in the gravy

definitions.meaning: Robert, the Victorian poet who wrote 'My Last Duchess' and married Elizabeth Barrett
a caramel colouring added to gravy to darken it

explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the poet Robert, and a colouring agent for gravies.

clue.text: Town of the old style Brunel railway termini

parts.note: OS is the standard abbreviation for old style, as in dates before the calendar change
Isambard Kingdom Brunel engineered the Great Western Railway, so his line gives the word west

indicators.note: the termini are the end stations, so take the first and last letters of the word railway

explanation.surface: A town is described by its old-fashioned Victorian station at the end of Brunel's line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Termini' looks like railway stations; it picks the first and last letters of 'railway'. Oswestry is a market town in Shropshire near the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: Oswestry is a market town in Shropshire, England.

clue.text: Doing or doing in

definitions.meaning: killing, especially putting to death by law

explanation.definitionFit: It means both performing a task and putting someone to death.

clue.text: Most pacific town in England

parts.note: 'pacific' suggests peaceful, but the Pacific Ocean was once called the ..., so the town's name is the old ocean name

explanation.surface: The most peaceful town in England is sought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pacific' looks like peaceful; the Pacific was formerly known as the South Sea. The town is a seaside resort district of Portsmouth, Hampshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort town forming part of Portsmouth on England's south coast, sharing the old name of the Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Old battleaxe takes a point at the current bridge game

parts.note: S, south, is one of the compass points
a pontoon is a bridge floated on the current of a river, and also the card game twenty-one

explanation.surface: A formidable old woman wins a point at the bridge table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old battleaxe' suggests a formidable woman, but it is an old weapon. PONTOON does double service as a floating bridge and the card game, so one leaf gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: A spontoon was a short pike or halberd carried by infantry officers in the eighteenth century, a weapon like a battleaxe.

clue.text: Men who bow may do so in this predicament?

definitions.text: Men who bow may do so in this predicament

parts.words: Men who bow may do so in this predicament
parts.note: obsequious people bow and drag a foot backwards; the same word is slang for a tight spot

explanation.surface: Courtiers are asked whether they must bow in an awkward situation.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'bow and scrape' means behave fawningly; the second verb is also a noun for an awkward predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: A difficult situation or fix; also the backward foot movement accompanying a deferential bow.

clue.text: How one foiled beasts tending to stray?

definitions.meaning: fought with foils, the light swords of the sport of swordplay
said of animals that wander: they are kept in by a barrier

explanation.definitionFit: Fenced means both having fought with a sword and enclosed behind a barrier.

clue.text: A fault that makes me tired

indicators.note: the words that follow are what the letters are made into, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone complains of a failing that wears them out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' rearranges the letters of ME TIRED.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark against someone for a failing or misconduct, the opposite of a merit.

clue.text: 9 let us give Surtees' plain alternative

parts.note: the answer to 9 across is a telephone, and to ring is to telephone someone
let's is the contraction of let us

explanation.surface: A caller suggests offering a plainer option to the novelist Surtees.
explanation.walkthrough: R. S. Surtees, the Victorian hunting novelist, wrote 'Plain or Ringlets?', so the alternative to plain in his title is this.
explanation.definitionFit: In Surtees's novel title the choice offered against plain hair is curled locks.

clue.text: The nearest place that's barred

definitions.meaning: the nearby or neighbourhood one, as an adjective used as a noun
a pub, a place with a bar, one's neighbourhood pub

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for the nearby pub, a building with a bar; as an adjective it means nearby.

clue.text: Practice ? Won't hear of it

parts.note: an established practice is the very thing that forbids something, as in 'tradition won't allow it'

explanation.surface: Someone flatly refuses to go along with a proposed practice.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word is a straight definition, and the rest describes what convention does when it rules something out: it won't hear of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Established usage or habit, which can forbid things by tradition.

clue.text: Past, present or future tight as ever!

definitions.meaning: these are grammatical categories of verb time
stretched taut, or nervous and strained

explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical tense is a verb form for time; as an adjective it means taut or strained.

clue.text: Port makes singer lose his sound quality

indicators.note: the singer loses something, so those letters are taken away from the word

parts.note: a baritone is a male singer with a middle voice
tone is the quality of a sound or voice

explanation.surface: A singer's voice deteriorates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose' removes TONE from BARITONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bari is a seaport on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy.

clue.text: Terror of a piper

parts.note: the piper is the Greek god Pan, whose sudden shouts were said to cause wild fear in the countryside

explanation.surface: A bagpipe player is struck by fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piper' suggests a bagpiper; it is Pan, the god of the pan-pipes, from whose name the word for sudden fear comes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden overwhelming fear, named after Pan, the pipe-playing Greek god.

clue.text: Quire-master?

parts.note: a quire is a set of sheets of paper, so a master of quires is a seller of paper, punning on choirmaster

explanation.surface: A choirmaster is named, with a misspelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quire' sounds like choir, suggesting a church musician; a quire is 24 or 25 sheets of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in paper, pens and office supplies, who deals in quires of paper.

clue.text: What's that unsubmerged red thing in the sea? It's a liability

parts.note: something not submerged is floating on the surface
being in the red means owing money, so the red thing is what is owed

explanation.surface: Someone at sea spots a red object bobbing on the waves and calls it a hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: The red thing in the sea pictures a buoy; red is the accountant's colour for money owed.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-term borrowing, such as government bills, not funded long-term, which a body owes and so counts against it.
